utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Mr. Re, is it, who is going to lead this next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will be leading the next witness, who will be Witness A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, I just wish to introduce by associate, Mr. Mirko Mrkic, who will today represent with me the defence of General Strugar. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. We noticed that Mr. Rodic has somehow adjusted his outward appearance. Are we getting the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please take the affirmation from the card that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness A. I'm going to show you a piece of paper with your name and date of birth on it. I'd just like you to -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you -- I'm afraid I can't hear you. I can't hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can I have that piece of paper back for a moment. I want to substitute it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now, thank you. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness A, can you please just look at that piece of paper. It has your name and your date of birth on it. Can you please confirm that those details are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence as an exhibit under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be Exhibit P93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness some personal details, so could we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you mobilised in 1991, Witness A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Not in 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At the end of January, after the Republic of Croatia gained recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what year was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you a civilian in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were living at Izmedju Polaca number 10. Is that -- and that's in the Old Town. Can you please describe to the Trial Chamber -- I'm sorry. I withdraw that. I just want to go back in time a little bit. Were you in Dubrovnik in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you living in the Old Town in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I started living in the Old Town since the 11th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to the Old Town in November -- to start living there in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the 11th of November was when there was strong shooting in the eastern part of town around the Belvedere Hotel, which was in fact the last line of Dubrovnik's free zone territory, the last boundary. And because of the strong shooting or shelling, the whole of the eastern Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. section of Dubrovnik was evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you living before the 11th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From the 7th of October until the 11th of November, I lived where I worked at my job in the Benedictine monastery called Sveti Jakov, St. Jakov.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there was heavy shelling on the 11th of November. Why did you move from the Benedictine monastery outside the Old Town into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Because it was impossible to continue living under shelling of that kind. And so all the people that lived in Sveti Jakov, Zlati Potok [phoen] and that general area moved towards the western district of the Old Town and other parts of town too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to the Old Town instead of some other place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Since ancient times, there are fortifications, stone shelters in the Old Town. And as the Old Town is under UNESCO protection, I thought it would be safest to go to the Old Town, because most probably the army would not open fire and target the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to describe for the Trial Chamber the building in which you went to live in November 1991. How many levels did it have, starting from the street to the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From the ground floor to the top with -- including an attic, or loft, five levels. That is to say, four levels, plus the area under the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was on the ground floor, that's the first level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: To the right of the building, which belonged to Mr. Ivo Brandjelica, on the ground floor was a coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To the left, what was on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Some sort of shop selling goods, textiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the left or right side of the building? Witness A, we might have to redact something there. Please be aware we're in open session, and Your Honours will make a direction for that to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The name of the witness's wife will be redacted. Is that all that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described two sides of the building, the left and the right side of the building. Was your wife living on the left or the right side, as you stand facing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: If we stand in front of the building looking at it from the northerly side towards the facade, it would be on the right, the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the next floor up, which is the third level of the second floor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the third level -- the third level was the one I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next level up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That was empty, just like the attic or loft.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the other side of the building, the left side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, on the third floor, there was a lady called Milica Aleksic. And most of the time, she lived with us afterwards and would go back to her building occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that call for further redaction, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just the witness's name that's the identifying feature, not the building itself or its occupants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How old was Ms. Aleksic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: She was about 75 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about in the attic? Was anyone living in the attic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Mrs. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a plan, a map, which is a copy of P13. I just want you to draw on it from above, sketching where your building was, and mark it with a large A.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you also, on top of where you've marked the A, which is on Stradun, with an arrow pointing to a block -- which is to the north of Izmedju Polaca, I want you to hatch in where your building was, as if you were looking at it from above.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The building there, is that number 10, or were there other numbers such as 8, 9 and 10 in that particular block? You've circled a whole block on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Moving from the main square Orlandov Stup towards the west on the right-hand side are the even numbers, and on the left-hand side the odd numbers. The first number was number 8, Milica Aleksic, and the one I lived in was number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it the same building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Physically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 8 to 10 occupies the entire street, as you've circled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Two entrances to the residential part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'll just leave the map there for the moment. We'll come back to it a bit later. On the top floor you've described there being an attic. Did the attic have windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were two so-called belvederes which looked out on to the Stradun, the northern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Belvederes, are they those open windows which are characteristic of Dubrovnik, like --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the second level of the right-hand side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you spend the night of the 5th of December, 1991, in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Mrs. Aleksic, did she spend that night with you as well or in your wife's -- what I meant was in your wife's flat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: For 15 days already, she was with us -- together with us before that, 15 days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you wake up on the morning of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I was woken up by the explosions far off, which kept coming nearer, nearer, and could be heard louder and louder, and that was around 5.00 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to describe to the Trial Chamber the explosions that you heard when you woke up, like how far away they sounded and the intensity of them and the -- or the time distance between the explosions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were sort of stifled explosions. They probably -- the shells fell around the ramparts, the walls of the Old Town. And to begin with, the intervals were longer between two shells, but gradually these intervals were shortened and they came fast, one after another. I couldn't actually tell you the time of these intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was yours and your wife's and Mrs. Aleksic's reaction to the shelling? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As the explosions became increasingly frequent, the first thing to do was to find the safest possible place in the apartment. And we decided that the bathroom was the safest place because it was middle. It was a small bathroom with just a shower and located in the central part of the apartment. So that's where we went. Mrs. Aleksic and my wife and I myself, most of the time, spent our time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you say how long you spent there, in the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, from 5.00 o'clock in the morning -- I think it was about 6.00 o'clock actually when the shells started falling right around the building itself. So say from 6.00 o'clock until 7.00 o'clock. Mrs. Aleksic and my wife were indoors all the time. When there were explosions that were obviously further away from the building, then I would peek through the window to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did the explosions and the shelling continue throughout that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From 6.00 o'clock practically every second, every other second, a shell would fall in various places within the old walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you see when you peeked out the window? And are you talking about the window on to Stradun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the window I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you see when you looked out that window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw construction material falling from the roofs, from the buildings, tiles, bricks, stone. This kept falling all the time right next to the buildings and further on towards the middle of Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How would you describe the intensity of the explosions as they continued throughout the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The explosions were terrible. One followed another. The buildings were shaking as if there was an earthquake going on. There was smoke everywhere. There was dust everywhere. There were these blazing lights coming in through the window. To put it quite simply, it was hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What could you smell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The smell of burning and of gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your building hit by anything during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the roof hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The roof was hit sometime between midday and 1.00 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what happened to your roof.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I knew the roof had been hit, because the building was shaking all the time. And every time the roof was hit, the house shook so badly as if it were an earthquake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times did you feel an impact to your house that felt as if something was hitting it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The entire roof was hit, and also part of Mrs. Aleksic's roof. And I could count three hits distinctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know a person called Pavo Urban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I knew him from town. Pavo Urban was a professional photographer. He was involved in artistic photography. And, among other things, he photographed all the damage due to the shelling. I had my father's camera, and he moved all about town. And the first time I met him was in St. Jakov. I knew him from before, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said you had your father's camera. Did you do something with your father's camera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have about 40 minutes of video footage recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see Pavo Urban on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Around 2.00 o'clock, when I heard the voices of his colleagues, other photographers, who were standing in Uska Street on the corner to the west of my building. They were talking in loud voices. They sounded panic-stricken. They were saying, Pavo was hit, Pavo was hit. That moment I ran to the window. I recognised Mr. Miro Kerner and Mr. Djukic who are also involved in photography. Miro Kerner died a few years ago. Then I looked to the right and below the city bell tower, I saw the body. It was lying on the ground without moving at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Urban's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I heard what they were saying. I myself could not recognise the face of the victim from such a long distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What position was the body lying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He was lying on his left hip and -- as if he were crouching, facing the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you a photograph. Before I show you the photograph, Witness A, can you tell the Trial Chamber what Mr. Urban was wearing when you saw him -- when you say the body -- when you saw the body lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He had a vest that he usually used, because it had a lot of pockets where he kept his films and other material he needed. That was his favorite vest that he used most of the time. It was very dark-coloured. It was civilian clothing at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about his trousers? Can you recall what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Jeans, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have a look at a photograph the usher is about to show you. Can you identify the person in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From this nearby, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Pavo Urban.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is Mr. Urban wearing the same clothes in that photo that you saw him wearing when you saw the body on the ground on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From that far away, the colours could not be discerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the -- what he's got on his top. What's he -- what is Mr. Urban wearing in the -- on his top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: A camera behind his left hand -- oh, yes, as far as clothing is concerned, it's the vest. It was not the vest he wore every day. This is red.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To the top left of that photograph, there is some building structure. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: This is a passage below the city bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is that where you saw the body lying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be marked as Exhibit P94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do after you saw Mr. Urban's colleagues gathered around the body, saying he'd been hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At that time the shells were falling at such a great intensity, that is to say, between midday and 2.00 o'clock. His colleagues would have had to risk their lives, and they certainly would have gotten killed themselves, had they tried to drag him away and had they run up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do? You looked out the window, you saw his colleagues there, what did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I looked out of the window to the right, I saw the body, and then I went back and I told my wife that Pavo was hit and that I would try to move him away from there. However, she started crying and she said, "No, you'll get killed." I went to the window again. Underneath the window at that moment there was an ambulance that was passing by. And I watched all of it. They came to him, and then I went back to my wife and I said that an ambulance had come and that I would not go. When I went back to the window again, I looked right, and I did not see the body any longer, and I did not see the ambulance any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you attend Mr. Urban's funeral?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: These were times of confusion. I got there, but I was actually late. There weren't any obituaries, there weren't any newspapers. So basically I was late for the funeral. There weren't many people. There was still shelling even during those days up there, so the cemetery was actually exposed. It was hard at any rate to bury people day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to turn to the map which is on your left and mark with a circle, a large one, and the letter B where you saw Mr. Urban's body lying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the record reflect the witness has drawn a circle between 14 and 15 on the western side -- sorry, the eastern side of the map and has marked it a B. Now, Witness A, can you please down the bottom right hand of the map, can you please write "Witness A." If you can write it in English, it would help, W-i-t-n-e-s-s A, and put today's date on it, which I believe is the 8th of March. All right. I'm going to show you another plan before we leave that. It's a copy of P17, which is an overhead photograph of Dubrovnik. I want you to use a finer pen and please do the same, mark with an A and a circle and arrow -- if you put an A at the top, an arrow down, and a circle where your house is -- was in 1991. And a B where Mr. Urban's -- where you saw Mr. Urban's body.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And please also write "Witness A" in the margin and the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May those two documents be received into evidence, firstly the map and secondly the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map and the photograph will be separately received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be Exhibit P95. And the photograph P96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness A, you described earlier feeling three detonations to your house. Can you remember approximately for how long the shelling continued, if at all, after you saw Mr. Urban's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The most intensive shelling was from 6.00 -- actually, I told you it started at 5.00. That's when I first registered the explosions. And then from 6.00 onwards, the shelling became continuous. From midday until 2.00 or 3.00 o'clock, there was hellish shelling. And then around 2.00 o'clock, Pavo Urban was killed -- or actually I heard voices that it was Pavo that had been hit. And I saw the body around 2.00 o'clock. And the last projectiles fell around 8.00 o'clock, 8.00 o'clock at night. And from 6.00 p.m. until 8.00 p.m., the shelling was subsiding considerably, but explosions could still be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you manage to inspect the damage to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Around 7.00 o'clock voices could be heard in the street. I saw that fire trucks had entered town. They were putting out fires, because there were buildings that were burning. I went down around 8.00. I went out and walked along Stradun. Quite simply, it was difficult to pass through Stradun. It was dark. There were no lights except from the lights coming from the fire trucks and from the blazes in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about the damage to your house? When did you manage to have a look at the damage to your house and see what had happened to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I went out then in the dark, and the explosion had quite simply opened the roof. The left belvedere had been destroyed. And next to it I saw some other damage that was sustained by the roof. So then it was obvious that there had been two hits. On the sofa, I found the stabiliser fin of a mortar shell. So it was the back part of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the calibre of the stabiliser shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Later on I found out, because in January I was mobilised. And at these mortar positions, I had occasion to hold an entire 120-millimetre mortar shell in my hands. And then I saw that it was that calibre. And I saw it in relation to my own hand, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any holes in your building or in the roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. There was great damage. One of the belvederes, the western one, was completely blown out. And westward, there was a concentric circle that was part of that belvedere window, and then there was a smaller circle that had blended into the bigger circle. So I realised that there had to have been two projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "two projectiles," are you saying two different sized projectiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. There were two projectiles of different size calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you found a stabiliser fin on a sofa. Where was this sofa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: This sofa was right below that belvedere. It was leaning on the wall, the western wall. And this stabiliser burned a hole in the sofa as it fell. And thank God that it didn't set fire on the sofa itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a clip of a video, which is of P78, from time marker 20 minutes to 22 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what I want you to do is point out to the Trial Chamber if you see your house in 1991 [sic]. You've stopped at 20:16 on the timer. What do you see? There's a building on the left of the clip.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There appears to be a laneway. Is that your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's Uska Street, where I go into from the Stradun, and it's opposite the residential part of the building. And this entrance here is the entrance to the coffee bar, and it's still a coffee bar today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've stopped at 21:51 on P78. What do you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In front you can see the bell tower of the town. And to the right, the first building, and the second building is my building. And up on top you can see the belvedere windows that were completely destroyed. The larger one is, in fact, the belvedere that was completely shattered by the explosion; to the west of it was a smaller one, a smaller hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you see the spot on that building where you saw Mr. Urban's body -- I'm sorry. I said "building," I meant on the street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Underneath the archway to the passage on the left-hand side of the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And does that video clip which we've just shown you depict the state of the Stradun in the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 7th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At this point in time, the street had been cleaned considerably. There was far more debris before. And the vehicles couldn't move around at all, nor could the pedestrians. There was a sort of passageway through the centre, but the vehicles couldn't get through. And as you see it now, this is already considerably cleaned up, the large portions of rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that video clip be received into evidence as a separate exhibit,, that is, the clip of P78 from time 20 minutes to 22 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That clip will be Prosecution Exhibit P97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe whether there was damage to other buildings in Izmedju Polaca from the shelling on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Quite simply, there wasn't a single building in the Old Town which was not destroyed, at least in part. Either the facade or the roof or some part of it. Everything was destroyed more or less, each one. Some more, some less.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about in your own street, Izmedju Polaca, are there any buildings there that you can describe to the Trial Chamber as having sustained particular damage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. All the buildings that were on fire, they burnt down. I know their locations. Some names I might not know, but I do know the buildings and in fact where they're situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your own street, Izmedju Polaca, where you were living in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. More or less all the roofs had been damaged, some by direct hits, others by indirect ones, hits to the facade, and so on. It was impossible to -- for them to remain in tact after all those projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any authorities inspect the damage to your building, that's 8 to 10 Izmedju Polaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Immediately after these occurrences, a week to ten days afterwards, after the 6th, expert teams from the conservation museum and institute for the protection of cultural monuments came by to investigate and assess the damage. I assumed they recorded the damage professionally in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you an extract of a report, which is MFI 51. I'm going to show you, for the record, pages 01069560, 01069561, 01069562, with accompanying draft translations. Turning to the first page, Witness A, that's 01069560, it's a report of an inspection of Izmedju Polaca 10 on the 13th of December, 1991. I want you to go to description of damage and just read that to yourself for a moment. You've read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness A, the first sentence: "The direct blow," et cetera, is that a correct description of the damage to the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please read the next sentence beginning: "In the attic," and likewise, is that a correct description of the damage to your building on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The third sentence -- sorry, sentence, "Shattered window panes," and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one: "Damage is done to the door and window frames," and so on, is that a correct description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the last sentence: "The same facade had damages of window panes in all the upper storeys." Is that a correct description of the damage you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next paragraph is headed "Estimate of Damage."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ignoring the last two words which are category 2. Is what is written there a correct description of the damage to your building on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next part is miscellaneous remarks: "A stabiliser of the projectile was found in the attic," which you've already described in evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please turn to the next page, 01069561.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I point out to Your Honours, it's a draft translation. There appears to be an error in the second category, which is location. It's 8 in the original and the translation has a 10 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again, please just read to yourself a description of the damage. Is Izmedju Polaca 8, is that the left-hand side of the building where Mrs. Aleksic lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Going to the first sentence of description of damage: "A direct hit to the roof -- at the roof," et cetera, is that a correct description of what occurred and the damage that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next sentence: "Damaged occurred in the attic," and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next sentence: "On the northern facade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the last sentence in that portion in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honours notice on the draft translation it appears that there has been a cut and paste from the previous page with damages done to the door and window frames. It seems to have been cut from the other page. We'll have that attended to and have the translation revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Go to the next category, which is -- or next paragraph headed estimate of damage. Just ignoring the last two words, category 2. Is that a correct description of the damage to the left-hand side of the building facing Stradun? It's number 8.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And underneath that it's miscellaneous and (remarks) and it says: "One small shrapnel and a 120-millimetre piece of the projectile stabiliser were found in the attic." What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next page, please, is 01069562. It has -- it's a -- it is a photograph. Is that a photograph on the left of number 8 and on the right of number 10, Izmedju Polaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: This is the facade of the building, looking at it from the Stradun side to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described looking out of a window and seeing Mr. Urban's body. Is that window in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, the right building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that's the window above the arched door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Above the right door, yes, with the arch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And so that we can identify this particular exhibit, can you please write on the front "Witness A," and the date on the front page of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence, too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P98, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And for the record, I indicate the damage described refers to the building described at page 3137 in the running page number of Schedule 2 to the Amended Indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness A, were you aware of the UNESCO protected status of the Old Town in October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Even the smallest child knew that. Everybody knew that living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any obvious signs in the Old Town during that period to show that it was a UNESCO protected World Heritage Site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Up on Minceta fortress, which is the most dominant within the Old Town, or over the Old Town, was the UNESCO flag that was flying. And on certain dominant buildings as well within the Old Town, you would see signs on many places, many buildings. Specific dark blue UNESCO signs, which testified to the category and the value of each particular building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what effect, if any, did the flying of these banners or signs or flags have on the morale of the people of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It had a positive psychological effect on everybody. However, the people thought quite blindly, unfortunately, that this fact would prevent any shelling of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In October, November, December 1991, did you see any military presence in the Old Town in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. There was no military presence in the Old Town at all. If a soldier happened to enter, he would enter without any weapons, and he was entering probably because he lived there. That would be the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've told the Trial Chamber you were a civilian. Was your wife a civilian in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was her occupation --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: She was. Everybody was more or less a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your wife's occupation in 1991, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: She's a qualified cook, and she worked at the Libertas Hotel, which was badly damaged like many other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the age range of the people living in the area in which you lived in, in the Old Town, that is around Izmedju Polaca? Young? Old? In between?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Most people in the Old Town were elderly persons. Those who weren't able to leave the town on time before it was blocked. Of course there were people of different ages, but mostly I would say elderly people, senior citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. That will obviously be a convenient time for a break. We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. A, I am Defence counsel. My name is Vladimir Petrovic, and I am going to be putting some questions to you in relation to your testimony in court today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. A, how was it that you established contact with the investigators of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They telephoned me and they asked me whether I wished to make a statement, and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who it was that called you and when this happened, of course if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do not remember the full name. But he did take a statement from me, a gentleman who is a Pakistani. I don't know. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us where it was that you gave this gentleman, this investigator, your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me where this exactly took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The Kompas Hotel in the Babin Kuk area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigator, the gentleman, on the -- on that occasion that you required protective measures in order to be able to testify before the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Not then, because at that time I wasn't employed by this company yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you told my distinguished colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor that you wished to testify with full protective measures before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It was, say, in mid-December when they first contacted me and they said that they wished for me to testify here. But that was my precondition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell my colleagues exactly what the reasons were why you wanted to testify under protective measures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, I told them exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I move on to my next questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to read the statement you gave to the gentleman from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did not, because I was told that I could not get a copy, either in Croatian or in English because those were the regulations of the court. The first time I read the statement was when I first came here in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, when you made this statement in the year 2000, was this statement read out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It was simultaneously interpreted from English into Croatian, but it was not translated in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you listen carefully to what the interpreter was saying? Did you have any objections then in 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, like to your colleagues this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they include these objections of yours in the text of the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So everything that is contained in this statement and that you read obviously when you came here to The Hague, does it exactly refer to everything you said in 2000 to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I think that this is a very superficial translation into the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So all possible mistakes are due to the translation. There are no material mistakes in terms of your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. Most of the mistakes have to do with grammar and style.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please be so kind as to tell us then -- or rather, tell the Honourable Trial Chamber where it was that you lived in 1991 until these events took place, the ones that we have been talking about here today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In 1982 we had finally completed our family house in Cilipi, near Dubrovnik airport. My parents, my younger sister, and I came to Cilipi to live there together. I entered university in 1979, 1980, and that's when we started building this house. And then we finally finished it by 1982 -- or rather, in 1982 I was registered officially at that address. Before that, I was registered in Rumbovci [phoen] in the municipality of Rama in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So since 1991 you have been living in Cilipi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the political situation like in Croatia in that year, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I am not a professional politician, but it was very confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you together with the other inhabitants of Cilipi already in the summer of 1991 started organising yourselves so that you could protect your area from enemy attacks, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That is correct. We were not mobilised. We were self-organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What else was it that you did in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I worked in the institute at St. Jakov.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do with the other citizens of Cilipi in terms of organising the defence, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Since we did not have any significant defence equipment, we just stood guard and we were to -- we were trying to prevent a surprise attack from the enemy, either from land or sea. That's the only thing we could do. Our hands were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the development of the political situation forced people in Cilipi to organise themselves in order to defend their area. Now, how did you intend to defend your area when you started organising yourselves in Cilipi? What form did that take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, the answer emerges from what I said a moment ago, from my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who was in charge of this organisation of defence? Who organised Cilipi's defence, and I'm talking about the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Nobody was in charge, because nobody did that in an organised fashion at all. We would do it based on our own instincts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that in the summer of 1991 you were organised, but you didn't have any organisational structure, nobody in charge, nobody at the head of all this, issuing orders, making decisions, that kind of thing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, please, how were you able to put your defence assignments into practice if there was nobody to head you, to lead you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We just monitored the situation, waited to see what was happening. Then we would tell the elderly and infirm to take refuge, those who wanted to take refuge, but quite a lot of people stayed on, even during the occupation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of the HDZ at Cilipi at that time, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of the local department at Cilipi office at Cilipi at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can't remember that either. It was a long time ago, 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police at Cilipi at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There wasn't a police station at Cilipi. There was just the police station in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police at the airport then at Cilipi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said - and I'm talking about page 2 of your statement and it is paragraph 5 - that: "Everyone," and we're talking about the period before October 1991, "all the younger people from my village, all young men from the village between the age of 16 to 60 were mobilised." That's how your sentence reads. Please let me finish and ask my question. Is that true? How many people and who mobilised them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That is an erroneous translation from Croatian into English. Nobody was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just ask that my learned friend put the complete sentence to the witness, which reads: "All young men from the village between the age of 16 to 60 were mobilised, and their weapons were hunting rifles. The total number of men mobilised from Cilipi was about 50." If he could put that to the witness rather than just take parts of a sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask that my microphone not be switched on -- switched off, if that doesn't present a problem to the technical booth. Now, Your Honours, in the B/C/S version of this statement, and that is the mother tongue of this particular witness, this section is divided into three separate sentences. I quoted the first sentence from that set of sentences, and I was just about to quote the second sentence and the third sentence. And I wasn't intending to mislead the witness. And anybody looking at the B/C/S version of the witness statement will be able to see that for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. And I was also going to observe that the core of your question was the issue of mobilisation, and that, I think, is what you're focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. A, why, what was happening at Cilipi during that period of time you don't denote as being mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, when you say "mobilisation," I think of a state in the name of defence or, rather, defence activities or aggressive activities for that matter, mobilised the military-able men. And I'm sure you're well aware of that. I'm sure your protege is well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All we did was to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement from the year 2000, the word "mobilised," as mentioned on page 2, you repeat three times. You say: "All young men from my village between the ages of 16 and 60 were mobilised." Then you say a little later on: "As far as I know, our village went into mobilisation independently of others." And then on that same page, you mention "mobilisation" for the third time. On page 3 of your statement you also mention it. When you speak about Ivan Rados you say he was mobilised. Then again on page 5 of your statement you say: "When the situation in Dubrovnik deteriorated, the local Croats mobilised into a struggle against the enemy." So why now do you think it's a problem for you to confirm that people were in fact mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I think it's just the wrong translation from English into Croatian. Or Serbian, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about mobilisation appeals over Radio Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was mobilisation ever proclaimed in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Mobilisation in Dubrovnik was proclaimed, and that was when I myself was mobilised. That is to say, towards the end of January 1992, after Croatia had been recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling this Honourable Trial Chamber that the Republic of Croatia in 1991 did not proclaim a state of general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Perhaps it did, but not in that area. It wasn't functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What particular assignments did you have in Cilipi, as you yourself say, in organising a defence? You yourself, what did you do specifically? What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Specifically speaking, when night fell for two or three hours I would be on duty at Konavli Stijena, the cliffs on our beach there, to monitor the movement of ships, vessels, if there was any, among other things, but just to observe this. I was there to observe any movement on the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And if you should happen to notice a ship, who would you inform? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Then I'd tell my colleagues, and then we would decide what to do, whether to inform people in -- go from house to house informing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many times did you actually notice any ships, vessels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: While I lived in Konavle, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What else were you able to observe from this vantage point of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We weren't in one spot. We moved around within a radius of one or two kilometres in the different villages, settlements, and part of Cilipi, Cilipi being the largest village in the then-Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that means that all the inhabitants of Cilipi between the ages of 16 and 60 were involved in this activity that you have described for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As they saw fit, according to their own instincts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many military-able men were there between the ages of 16 and 60 at Cilipi at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, give us a rough estimate then, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, the number I mentioned, about 50, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far towards the Montenegrin border did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I personally, with this group from Cilipi, the furthest I went to was Radovcici, the village of Radovcici to the east, which is about three kilometres eastwards, or in a south-easterly direction with respect to Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st of October, did you -- I'm asking you about before the 1st of October. How far did you and your unit go or group of people from Cilipi? What was the furthest it went to the east?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I said within a radius of about one to two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, from this furthest point that you reached, how far was it to the Montenegrin border, both to the west and to the east and to the north?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The Montenegrin border stretches in the direction of north/south, if you're looking at it from the Konavle aspect, roughly. Now, the village of Radovcici that I mentioned is about five kilometres away, up to Debeli Brijeg specifically or Vitaljina and the peninsula to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's be more specific and precise. What I asked you was: Before the 1st of October you told us you had gone to -- within a radius of two kilometres from Cilipi. Now, this furthest point from Cilipi, how far is that point to the Montenegrin border. Radovcici is five kilometres from your village you said. So how far is the furthest point you reached from Debeli Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Six kilometres roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what were you able to see from there? What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We couldn't see anything. We were on duty, kept watch. But we heard from stories that on the 23rd of September the JNA forces and the volunteers on the other side had crossed the Croatian border at Bani [phoen], Debeli Brijeg, and up there in the region of Dubravka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the 23rd of what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It was September, the ninth month, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you have told us that you saw nothing there, you did nothing there, you were just there and doing guard duty or on watch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, we didn't sit around; we walked around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why you told the investigators that you noticed movement of JNA units along the border belt. Where were you able to see that from, to observe that from, if you weren't close up by the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I heard that from people who were withdrawing, people who had assessed that the time had come for them to withdraw to the west towards Dubrovnik. And they passed through Cilipi, so we heard about that. And the first time I personally observed that was on the evening of the 5th at Radovcici. I saw a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am trying to ask you up until the 1st of October, and please tell me, up to the 1st of October is what you said: "We observed JNA movement along the border belt." You're talking about mobilisation, people ranging between 16 to 60, hunting rifles and so on. Up to the 1st of October. So I'm asking you where it was you were able to notice JNA movement up to that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: People who lived in the border villages talked about it, talked about noticing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you yourself did not actually see anything, although you say here that you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The wrong translation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what were you armed with up until the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I had my father's hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many armed persons were there in that group of yours of 50 men from Cilipi before the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, most people had some sort of long-barrelled weapon. Mostly they were hunting rifles, and somebody who might have purchased for their own money a carbine, which is a rifle with a bullet, M-48 calibre, if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, anybody in the region of Cilipi, did they have any military weapons at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Perhaps some people did -- well, some of them did. They had some sort of automatic rifle that they had purchased themselves, but that was rare, very few of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me please where one could purchase an automatic rifle at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, after the 1st of October now, up until, let's say, the 15th of October, during that period of time, what weapon did you personally have and what weapons did your group have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Hunting rifles, the military carbines, and military rifles of the M-48 calibre type.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that perhaps there were some organised Croatian forces in Dubrovnik. Do you know anything about organised Croatian forces in Dubrovnik itself at the period -- material period, that is to say, before the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. From mid-September we no longer went to work. And I was in Cilipi all the time. So after mid-September, I didn't go into Dubrovnik to work anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please tell us why it was that from mid-September you didn't go to work any longer? Because of your assignments in the Cilipi unit or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. Quite simply, we received orders from the academy that we weren't to go to work anymore for our own safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at this time that you're talking about now there was absolutely nothing going on in the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik, the town of Dubrovnik, in the month of September there was peace in the area. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were no physical military operations; that's true. But there was a war in Eastern Slavonia, and this did affect the population to a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did everybody stop working in Dubrovnik in mid-September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about your relatives, friends, your future wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, specifically my wife did work. She told me about it later; I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it was only the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts that stopped working in mid-September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That I know. The institute at Sveti Jakov.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since it stopped working, there was no need for you to go towards the town of Dubrovnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody from Cilipi go to the town of Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody perhaps talk about that? You were engaged in the defence of your village and your state. Were you not interested in what was going on in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I was interested. People talked about different things, but I think that this was so that they would not personally be afraid and that the morale would be high. I don't know whether these stories were correct, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me what the last sentence on page 2 means -- or rather, the first sentence in the last paragraph of page 2 of your statement where it says: "Together with the defenders from my area, I continued to resist the enemy aggression."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us then what it was that you meant when you said something that was obviously not what is written here. What was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I probably said, "Together with my colleagues, fellow citizens, we stayed on in Cilipi."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you said, "I stayed in Cilipi with my colleagues," and the interpreter translated it by saying: "Together with the defenders from my area, I continued resisting enemy aggression"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. The entire population that was attacked were actually the defenders, but they were organised in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now we are moving on to the period after the 1st of October. So there was no organisation, no units. There was nothing in the territory of Konavle and Cilipi as the biggest village in the area of Konavle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in your statement you said: "Along with other defenders from my area, I continued to resist the enemy aggression." And on the 25th of January this year, you said to my learned friends: [In English] "From my area. We continued to observe enemy movements as we had nothing to resist with. We reported to the villagers what was happening and were able to warn others." [Interpretation] Sir, why are you dodging the issue? Why are you avoiding telling the Trial Chamber that you were actively involved in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: If this is active defence, then it is true, what I described to you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If they did not understand you correctly the first time, my learned friends, did they understand you correctly the second time? Do you mean what you said this other time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: This is the same assertion, like the previous question you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Although this statement was read out to you, you did not say a word about any of this having been inaccurate, that you resisted aggression, that you defended yourself. If it is incorrect, it should not be part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did say that it was a mistranslation, that it was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 2002 -- in 2000 as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do not remember what I said in 2000. Do you remember what you were saying in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because I know that my colleagues work professionally and conscientiously. So I'm asking you this because I am quite sure that at that time you did not say anything to them. When you came here, you came to realise that it was not very good for you to have your role in all of this scene. You tried to present yourself as an innocent onlooker and that you did not do anything vis-a-vis the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's not correct. What you are saying is what you are saying, and I said what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Under whose command were you after the 1st of October in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Nobody's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody command this unit of 50 men from the region of Cilipi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We reached agreement together. We made conclusions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in some self-management manner you decided how you would defend your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Precisely, in a self-management manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a man called Nojko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of General Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of October onwards, were you under the direct command of Nojko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you move about after the 1st of October in the region of Konavle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I've already told you that, within a two-kilometre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in the village of Radovcici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: About 20 of us came along the coast to the hillocks around Radovcici. And at a distance of about 100 or 200 metres, we saw a column of different military vehicles. And pieces of equipment that were moving at a slow pace in the direction of Popovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us when did the JNA cross the border near Debeli Brijeg? When was that? Was it on the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it on that 23rd of September that you referred to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, between the 23rd of September and the 5th of October, what was actually going on? How many kilometres was the JNA supposed to travel over these two weeks and more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I said that Radovcici is about five kilometres away from the border, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So why did the JNA not cover this distance throughout that time? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The JNA probably knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody put up a resistance to the JNA in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: According to stories that were bandied about, there was some resistance in the area near the border. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And nobody else offered any resistance to the JNA units moving from Debeli Brijeg to Cavtat, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did not see any such thing myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the defence forces of the town of Dubrovnik were deployed in the village of Dubravka, the village of Bani, and Besbuja [phoen], Radovcici, Grude? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of the village of Besbuja. I know about the other villages, where they are, but I personally do not know about this fact that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Resnica is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can't remember now exactly. I do not know exactly where it is. But it sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's an elevation above Molunat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were two cannons there belonging to the Croatian army, 85-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did not see that. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us whether you know where Zvekovica is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Cavtat is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you go through Zvekovica as you travel to the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a position of the Croatian army over there perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were no weapons to mention, so you cannot really use the word "positions." And there was no such thing as the Croatian army at that time. The Croatian army was established after the recognition of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was a JNA tank destroyed in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: People were saying that an armoured vehicle had been hit in the area of Zvekovica, a vehicle belonging to the enemy forces, but I only heard about that. At that time I was in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was this tank damaged? By what? A hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably something more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, I put it to you that the defence forces, and you were part of them, were deployed in all these villages I mentioned just now, that you were under the direct command of the commander of the defence of the town of Dubrovnik, Nojko Marinovic, and that you actively participated in resisting the JNA units that were marching in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: My group, no. Perhaps other groups were under this command, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How big is this area, Mr. A, that you do not know anything, except about your own group, which was moving around quite a bit in that area? How many kilometres are there, so that you do not know what is going on in the neighbouring village right next to you, in the village of Zvekovica, too, which is a few kilometres away from your village, perhaps even less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Zvekovica is about two kilometres away from Cilipi, sort of. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come you know nothing about this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, I was an eye witness of the airplanes that were flying over the sea, and the airport was targeted at the time. I don't know what time of aircraft this was, but it flew over my house and the house was shaking. That's when the infrastructure at the airport was bombed. On the 1st of October, I heard that Srdj was targeted by missile attacks, and all these infrastructure facilities, like at Komolac and the transmitter at Srdj, and that's what I heard. On that day, the 1st of October, I was convinced myself of the fact that the gasoline station was destroyed at the airport and fuel containers were thrown about, scattered about the road, and the building was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. But the point is that you did not see any members of the national guards corps or the Croatian army. You didn't see any such thing. Is that the conclusion, to cut this story short?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were some people in camouflage uniforms, but these are people who obtained these uniforms somewhere on their own. But more or less these were people in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what did these people in camouflage uniforms do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, what the rest of us did. They were looking on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. "I remember that we took position in Radovcici, three kilometres away from Cilipi." What was it that you did then? You were looking on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We heard -- we heard that they were advancing, that the enemy forces were advancing along the road, the lower road, the one that runs parallel to the highway that goes from the north where this pass is. And these enemy forces were advancing from Prevlaka through these villages of Mikolici [phoen], Radovcici, and we heard that they were advancing. We came to Popovici, a village that is one kilometre west of Radovcici, and then on foot, on foot, we walked along the seacoast and came to the hillocks above Radovcici, and we saw for ourselves a column of different vehicles, military vehicles and many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the 20 of you went to Radovcici to reconnoiter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, to see how many enemy forces were there, how many enemy troops there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us, in order to observe why did 20 of you have to go? Wasn't it sufficient for one person to go and to inform the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, but psychologically a person feels safer if there's a bigger group involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So then in the presence of the heavily-armed JNA, you moved in groups of 20 so that you would feel safer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, but not along the road, but along the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say the following: "We saw many members of the JNA, some 150 to 200 metres from us. The enemy forces had already captured a part of the village and we could see them looting the houses. We could also see heavily-armed soldiers on the road with tanks, cannons, and other weapons. One of us fired a single shot, a single bullet, from the hunting riffle. And there was panic in the enemy force."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
