utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to explain to this Trial Chamber how heavily-armed soldiers in tanks, cannons, succumb to panic from one single shot that was fired from a hunting rifle. Could you please explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We were 150 to 200 metres away on a hillock. And the soldiers, a group of soldiers on a terrace in front of a house we saw, or I saw, that they were rolling barrels of wine out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you the following: How was it possible that the JNA, heavily armed and equipped with tanks, cannons, and other weapons, how were they in a panic when they heard one single shot fired from a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The people in the group would escape to the military vehicles. They went back to the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you after this single bullet had been fired from this one hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We scattered. We were divided into two groups, and then we scattered and we went back and took the same route we took when we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, if your assignment was to observe, why did you shoot from a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In order to see the reaction, to provoke reaction, on the part of the enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you shot this one single bullet from that hunting rifle, did they shoot at you from cannons, tanks, planes, ships", what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. They shot at us from light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But one bullet was enough, was it, to create this panic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw them rush back to their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to fire something else except for this one bullet from this one hunting riffle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that: "Along with these regular soldiers, I saw volunteers wearing civilian clothes, both Serbs and Montenegrins. I recognised them from their dialect, the way they spoke."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, how it was that from a distance of 200 metres you happened to recognise them as being Serbs or Montenegrins by the way they were speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were speaking loudly, shouting to each other, and of course each of the dialects in the territories of the former Yugoslavia have their characteristic features.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: "Jovo," "Bre," "more [phoen]," those are characteristic terms used by the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How were you able to distinguish between Serbs and Montenegrins from that vantage point of yours from which you were observing them? How were you able to distinguish who were Serbs and who were Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: By their speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who was in the majority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were far more soldiers in uniform. A very small number were the ones who were in some indistinguishable clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, from there did you take up a reserve position at Popovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. It was dark already, night-time, and we didn't have any means of communication. We've separated, as I already said, into two groups. And my group, which was made up of about ten men, took the south side of the village. It passed through the village and we entered a vineyard, where we sat down and took stock to see -- we saw the church up at -- on the hill of Popovici village. There was a church on fire, and we realised that enemy forces were round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to use your rifle there perhaps again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any need of using it anymore, nor did we use anything else. It was night-time already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, how did you know that the were soldiers from the Sava Kovacevic brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I heard about that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From people, the people I communicated with. We exchanged views, information, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where did you go on after that that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At about 2.00 o'clock we were sitting about in the vineyard, because we didn't dare get out on to the main road. We didn't have any orientation as to who was where. Our two groups might have killed each other in the darkness, not knowing who we were encountering. And as it was already cold at night and we were freezing, we had no choice, no way out, but to take the forest running parallel to the road and to move in the direction of Cilipi that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We passed through the forest and reached what we thought was a safe part of the road. Part of my group went to Cilipi, and I myself went to Cavtat because my sister was down there, and she was deployed by the Territorial Defence down there. She was in the Crisis Staff -- by the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik. She was sent to help out the refugees in the hotels in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now explain this to me, please: Your sister was sent by the Territorial Defence and Crisis Staff of the city of Dubrovnik, she was given an assignment and sent to Cavtat to perform that assignment, whereas you, yourself, alone, not organised, not having contacts with anybody, were observing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: She was working in the Dubrovnik pharmacies that belonged to the city of Dubrovnik. And they had authority over their workers, employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had no authority over you and your group then. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means you could have left your unit whenever you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who stayed on to do this observation work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know anymore who stayed on. Probably some other groups from other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know from what positions those other groups were able to do this observation work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you yourself left your group, and if they stayed on at Cilipi at the front line, I can just conclude that you fled from Cavtat. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any armed persons in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Anywhere along the road from Cilipi through Radovcici to Cavtat, did you happen to see any armed Croatian defenders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I went in my car, which was parked by my house. And I happened to pass some cars along the road. But it was night-time, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in these other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, they were civilian vehicles. There were some people inside; the cars were moving. So that means somebody was driving them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question to you was: Did you see any Croatian defenders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of October, you returned to Cilipi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then once again you heard enemy soldiers speaking the Serbian and Montenegrin dialects, but once again you say you didn't hear what they were actually saying. Is that right

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. They were inarticulated voices, but I did hear names characteristic of Serbs. And as soon as I arrived in Mocici, a village which is on the west --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Tell me this, please: How were you able, and which route did you take to reach your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Through the Dubrovacka Zupa, along the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, please -- because you and I are well aware of where that lies, but tell the Trial Chamber, please, from the 6th of October, from Cilipi, how many kilometres did you pass to reach your parents'?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I left at about 10.00 from the Albatros, from where my sister was, the hotel. And my aim was to find my group -- to meet up with my group in Cilipi, because they were sleeping in the cultural building over there. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You say they were sleeping in the cultural centre because they were actually people from Cilipi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they sleep in their own homes and disperse and scatter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were afraid. That's what they decided to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: When I reached Mocici, and you can see the church at Cilipi from Mocici --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I asked you how many kilometres you did, what length of road did you traverse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From Cavtat to Mocici, my house in Cilipi is about three kilometres. Afterwards from my house to Dubrovnik to Babin Kuk, the Argosy Hotel in actual fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many kilometres is that and where did you pass through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It's about 30 kilometres altogether, all the places I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far is hotel Argosy in Babin Kuk from Cavtat to the point you set out from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: About 25 kilometres from own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Throughout those 25 kilometres, going through Cavtat, the whole of the Dubrovacka Zupa area and the town of Dubrovnik, right up until Babin Kuk which lies to the west of the town of Dubrovnik, did you see any armed Croatian defenders on your route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw people with sparse weapons, hunting rifles. I did happen across quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So where did you meet these people out with hunting rifles? Where did you come across them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Mlini, Kupari, then around the hotel at Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints on this 25 kilometre-long route of yours from Cavtat through Zupa through town to Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In front of the hotel at Babin Kuk, no, there were no checkpoints. Just people on their own who initiative -- in Mlini, for example, a man stopped me to ask me where I was going. And he said, "You shouldn't go there, stay here with us." And I said I was going to my parents' place but hat I would return.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps try to prevent you going ahead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, he didn't try to prevent me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to get out of the town of Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik area, had you wanted to -- to leave that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. Because at that time, Dubrovnik was under siege already, in an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you have got on one of the ferries and leave the town that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The police wouldn't allow us to do that. They didn't allow military-able men to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us in view of the fact that there was no organised defence in the town of Dubrovnik itself, why then did the police prevent military-able men from leaving the down of Dubrovnik? What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Probably because they were military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But if there were no organised units, if there was no weaponry, if there were just a few hunting rifles, why would the police stop people from getting on to a ferry and leaving town and going to Split, Rijeka, wherever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 6th of October -- December, 1991, now please. Who attended the meeting of your colleagues, as you say, the defenders in Zvekovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: You want to know who was there? You want me to give their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as you're able to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. The group that I mentioned, of these ten or so men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us please what the names of these people that made up the group was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were all my neighbours from Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please give us their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I draw the knot [as interpreted], if I don't actually have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very important for us to hear the names in order to establish who the members of your group were and what the group's activities were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I've said that countless times what the activities of our group were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And I'm asking you to tell us please who the members of your group were and who was in command of your group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Nobody was in command; I've already said that. I said that we agreed together as to what we were to do. We made our own decisions and our own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have your assistance in this matter. Could you please ask the distinguished witness to give us the names of his group, the members of his group, the ones he worked with in the Cilipi area during the material time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to recall those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know all the last names in Cilipi, and these people bore those last names, Resetar, Pujo, Brajica, Obradovic, Simovic, Bete, and others. All of these are last names from Cilipi and from the area around Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did any one of those have any command, control, or authority over you in what you did as a group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no chain of command whatsoever. We reached agreement together and we reached decisions together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that sufficient for your purposes, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would just like to ask to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The people you mentioned consisted of your -- your group consisted of those people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And these people were at this meeting on the 6th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you decide there at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We decided to stay at Zvekovica. To stay there at Zvekovica to see what would happen afterwards. And we spent that night at Zvekovica. The next morning -- is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you did that night at Zvekovica? What was it that you continued doing at Zvekovica that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We were there to see whether the enemy army would reach Zvekovica, at which pace the enemy army was advancing from Radovcici and from the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Again, with these weapons that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go from Cavtat to Babin Kuk about 50 kilometres on the previous day with that hunting rifle of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you where it was that you were going armed like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that I went to -- that I was going to visit my family and get some water for them because there was a shortage of water at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you traversed these 25 kilometres in order to bring your parents water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right. And to tell them that I was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And there was no water anywhere closer to your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. There was a shortage of water at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then you say on the morning of the 7th of October: "We discussed the situation yet again and we realised that it was pointless to continue the resistance, as we were no match to the powerful and well-equipped JNA. So we discontinued the resistance against the enemy forces and split up." Let me try to interpret this properly. You gave up on continuing your observation, and then you split up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, why then did the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal write down here then that it was your understanding that it was useless to continue the resistance? How could this kind of a mistake happen in the translation, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't explain that to you. Ask the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does this second sentence mean? "So we discontinued the resistance against the enemy forces and split up."?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It means that we split up, that we parted our ways, everybody went his own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But what does this mean, to discontinue resistance, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It means that we realised that we could not put up any kind of resistance whatsoever. It was a cat-and-mouse game. We were totally unequal. We were nothing compared to the forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us summarise this, Mr. A. Your resistance from the 1st of October until the 7th of October ended on the 7th of October. And during those seven days, your group fired one single bullet, and from a hunting rifle at that, on the 5th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time do you think, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, in your statement you say the following: "Some defenders in Zupa Dubrovacka nevertheless continued to fight against the JNA. One of them was my relative, Ivan Rados." Did these people continue to fight while you left your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's the mistake? What is wrong in this sentence, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Their group was organised just like my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So yet again, you were totally misunderstood, both by the interpreter and by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were these people doing in Zupa Dubrovacka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Also observing the surrounding hills. Observing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed or were they also armed with hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Just like we were, poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone who in the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik and the town of Dubrovnik in the months of October, November, and December 1991 who was working actively in the field of defence against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I personally do not know about this, but I heard various stories. These stories were also a very psychological nature, in view of the persons who were actually telling the stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik and in the town of Dubrovnik, was there anyone who was organised in ZNG units, Croatian units, special units of the Croatian army, in the period of October, November, December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Maybe, but I am not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any of this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Only rumours, all sorts of rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. A, what was it that you heard about organised forces of the ZNG, the Croatian army, the special police, and the regular police in the town of Dubrovnik and in the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik, in view of these three months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I've already told you I heard different stories. I myself cannot say that they were authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what it was that you heard. I'm not asking you about authenticity. I asked you what it was that you heard, Mr. A.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I heard that we had some forces, that they couldn't do anything to us, that the world cares about Dubrovnik and doesn't want Dubrovnik to be occupied, that the 6th fleet was in the Adriatic, that they would not allow missile attacks on the entire area of Dubrovnik, let alone the Old Town, and stories to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you what it was that you heard about the defence forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: And I've given you an answer. I don't know anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So these people who were in Zupa Dubrovacka and who fell victim there were also observing. How were they armed; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said two minutes ago that these people in Zupa Dubrovacka were organised just like you. However, in your statement you say for Ivan Rados, your relative, he had been mobilised, and was assigned to the Dubrovacka Zupa area, he was stationed in the area of Mlini, and the commander of his group was a police officer, Ante Vulic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He was not mobilised; he volunteered. He joined that group voluntarily. And they functioned the way we did. Ante Vulic, the mentioned Ante Vulic, was a policeman in the former state as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, you say here: "The commander of his group was Ante Vulic." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That means that he probably knew somewhat more about the military, about warfare, about organisation, in view of the fact that he was a policeman. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this also a mistranslation, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So instead of this word "commander of his group," what were they supposed to say for this Mr. Vulic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That was my assumption; it was logical. My assumption, he was the most competent with the best professional training in terms of defence and organisation in general, since he was a policeman. So this was, in a way, part of his own line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph you again refer to Ante Vulic as the commander. You say: "Ante Vulic, his commander, was also injured one of those days but in a different attack." Was that a mistranslation as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, it was obviously the same translator/interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, do you know English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can use the English language. I have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the front page of your statement of the 14th and 18th of September, 2000, it says: "Languages spoken: Croatian and English." It says here that you speak Croatian and English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can use both languages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, did you intervene in this multitude of cases of mistranslation, because you understand both English and Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I understand Serbian, too. I had no time to intervene. I told you that this was translated verbally to me, that I did give my own comments, again verbally, and that it was the first time that I read this in the Croatian language in January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In these many cases of mistranslation, why did you not react on the spot? Didn't you realise that you were being mistranslated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't think it was that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think it's that important today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Afterwards when I read this, I analysed it and I took a position of my own with regard to this matter. Obviously it differed from that I took in the year 2000. A person learns throughout his life, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us where the Benedictine cloister is. Could you please describe the locality to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: East of the Old Town. As the crow flies, it's two kilometres away, near the Belvedere Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In October, November, December 1991, what was in the Belvedere Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did not visit the Belvedere a single time within that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the cloister, the monastery, where you worked, how far away is it from the Belvedere Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: About 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You never found out what was 200 metres away from the place where you lived and worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: With the late Pavo Urban, I came only once. I don't remember the exact date. It was probably the beginning of November. I came to -- in front of the main entrance of the Belvedere Hotel, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were you and Pavo Urban looking for there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We were recording with my camera and with his camera the damage that was caused by the projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to explain to us what you told us a while ago; namely, that in mid-September you left your place of work because such instructions were received from Zagreb from the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No. These were not instructions. This was a recommendation. They said that if working conditions were impossible, do not work until further notice -- or rather, until proper conditions are created.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Petrovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of October, why did you go back to your work place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In order to seek shelter, in order to have a place to go, a place to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say: "On the 7th of October, 1991, I returned to Dubrovnik at my work place in the Benedictine monastery and stayed there."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you work, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, I was there on my own, all alone, but there were some 20 or so people there too, whose assessment was that this was a much firmer building than their houses in Zlati Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were the Croatian positions of the Croatian army around the town of Dubrovnik in October, November, December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know, because I did not walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, were you, for instance, able to go to Kupari or Mlini?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the 7th, no, you couldn't pass by on the 7th. You couldn't go further from Mlini because that is the narrow stretch of border belt, the Croatian border belt. And from the hills above, people were there with snipers and other weapons, and they were targeting anybody who wanted to pass by that way and attempted to do so and get through to Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the last defence line was of the Croatian army on that eastern access towards Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I tell you that it was just 200 metres from the place you lived and worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Are you talking about Dubrovnik or Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, I'm talking about Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, that's a different story altogether. Behind the Belvedere, to the east of the Belvedere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I asked you a moment ago, and I asked you quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's what I heard, and I can tell you that I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what did you hear? What was there at the Belvedere Hotel, let me ask you again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about what was to be found in the Belvedere Hotel, but that people were patrolling the area behind the Belvedere Hotel. But I didn't see that take place personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were these people patrolling the region behind the Belvedere Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Probably the people from town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they belonged to any military unit, police unit? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I saw hunting rifles and things like that, simple types of weapons, nothing specific. And they were wearing civilian uniforms. Some I saw were in camouflage uniform, but others wore a combined form of civilian and camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These people by the Belvedere were doing the same thing that you were doing in Cilipi, observing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know what their function was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened up at Mount Srdj, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: October, November, December 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From my monastery with the camera I had that I've already mentioned, I recorded quite a number of explosions, attacks from the sea, from the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I just observed explosions and clouds of smoke, which were probably the result of the attack. But I don't know who attacked whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was up at Srdj, Mr. A, let me ask you again, during those three months. Just a brief answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I personally do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who during those three months was up at Zarkovica, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I think the enemy army had taken control of Zarkovica sometime in mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn of that, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Because they were targeting the island of Lokrum with their projectiles from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, how far is Zarkovica from the monastery itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As the crow flies, approximately 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you knew that at a distance of 400 metres were the positions of the enemy army; however, you did not know that at 200 metres there was the last line of the Croatian defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No projectiles were coming from that range of 200 metres, so I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, now these observers at the Belvedere Hotel on the Croatian side, did they ever shoot at anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever happen to hear any shots from those hunting rifles or whatever else they had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I heard shots, but I wasn't an eye witness to be able to tell you who did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, did they perhaps shoot from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, in the town of Dubrovnik, during these three months, see anything other than hunting rifles by way of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At that time, no. Later on in 1992, yes. In the Old Town, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian army perhaps during those three months in the town of Dubrovnik have any mortars, for example, cannons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I personally didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about such things perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, stories did go around about that in 1992, different rumours, but I didn't see that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why didn't the JNA enter the Belvedere Hotel or your monastery or the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: You would have to ask the JNA that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody between the town of Dubrovnik and the positions held by the JNA in the hills around the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you afraid, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, what specialty did you have from your JNA training days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft attack, light 92M systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you well-versed in the matter of weapons, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I understand those weapons very well, pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between a three-barrel anti-aircraft gun? Do you know what that looks like? Can you distinguish that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what does it look like? Can you describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, there are three barrels. The centre one is a little longer, but I assume the calibre is the same, 20 millimetres. That's as far as my knowledge goes. Of course I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see a piece of artillery weapon of that kind in the town of Dubrovnik in October, November or December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, not me. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else see that, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Perhaps. I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody ever shoot from the town of Dubrovnik, targeting JNA positions around the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Once again, after the establishment of the regular 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army in Dubrovnik, we exchanged opinions, compared notes. I did hear that somebody did shoot, but I just heard about that. I didn't see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, what you heard, what it was that you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, people said that there was a truck upon which this cannon -- anti-aircraft cannon was installed in order to create the impression of having some sort of stronger force, stronger defence force. And the truck moved from the eastern -- from the western to the eastern part of town. It would shoot a burst of gunfire several times to create this general impression, to create the noise and general audio impression of having a defence force by the people -- the forces around the hills who were able to hear that. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you never saw the likes of anything like that or heard it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw that cannon in 1992, in February, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go outside the monastery you were in, venture out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Outside? Only when there were no operations underway, when there was no shelling and shells falling around the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from the 7th of October until the 11th of November when you moved into the Old Town, was there shooting at the town of Dubrovnik and its surrounding parts every day? Did they take place on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Every day, but the intensity differed. There would be sporadic shooting, as one says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was the general alarm sounded every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: A general alarm would be sounded immediately after the first projectiles fell. And a siren would be sounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I asked you was: Was there a general alarm sounded every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On how many days between the 7th of October and the 11th of November was a general alarm sounded, denoting all out danger, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know the number of times, but many times certainly. I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume there were more days when the general alarm was sounded than the number of days when it wasn't sounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I would say in a ratio of 70 to 30 per cent. 70 per cent of the time the general alarm was sounded, and 30 per cent of the time it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As you said a moment ago that the general alarm would be sounded once the first projectiles had hit, that further means that 28 days during this period of time, or perhaps 25 days during that period of time, shells fell on the Old Town and the town of Dubrovnik. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking your conclusions are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give any thought to joining up the defenders, or rather, the observers who were stationed at the Belvedere Hotel and who were there observing the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. I would have joined them, but there weren't the conditions for me to do so. What could I join them with? With my own bare hands? I would have readily have joined them otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, where was your rifle, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: With me, at the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they too, sir, just had hunting rifles. Why didn't you join them then with your hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I was in the institute. There was no sense in it. It would carry not weight, going there with a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Some people stayed there to do their observing with their rifles, but you didn't join them. Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: My own personal choice. I don't know. We're all different, as you well know, and we react differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why then did you join up in the first -- in January 1992? Why did you join the defenders then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: My house was over there, and that was sufficient reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, your house was there in October and in November and in December as well. And you didn't join up, although you were armed, you had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Sir, I don't follow your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: I asked you why you joined the defenders in 1992, and your answer was because your house was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then I went on to ask you: Why didn't you join the defenders in October, November, and December of 1991, because your house was still there at that time, and you were armed, you had a rifle at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: You're right. In 1992, at the end of January, I was mobilised after the Croatian state had gained international recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you've told us for the third time now that you were mobilised after international recognition. What does that have to do with mobilisation at all in your participation and the defence of your house? What did those two things have in common?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: What did they have in common? Draw your own conclusions. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, Mr. A. Does that mean that you decided to join the army only when the state had been internationally recognised? Up until that time, you didn't consider it to be your duty or that you needed to? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, you are. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what did you think up until that time, up until 1992? Who should have defended your home, your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I should have done, but I didn't have anything to defend it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. What was it that you saw at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There was no direct view of Zarkovica from the monastery. From the Old Town, there is. At Zarkovica, there was a fortification dating back to the times of Napoleon. I'm talking to 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was there a fort like that on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. There was a fort on Srdj, too, called imperijal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can Srdj be seen from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when you saw Zarkovica from the Old Town, did you see Srdj, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And at Zarkovica you saw the JNA, and who was it that you saw at Srdj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I didn't see the JNA. I didn't. With the naked eye, you cannot see anything at such a distance. I saw the fortification that was probably used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Zarkovica is 400 metres from the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear anything from Zarkovica while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While you were at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Who were they shooting at, these people from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I already told you, the island of Lokrum and -- I mean, that's what I saw. In view of the reflections of the projectiles. In other places, I didn't notice that, whether the shooting actually came from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Tell me exactly what does your apartment look like, the one in the building at Izmedju Polaca number 10? Where is the entrance? From which street does one enter your apartment at Izmedju Polaca number 10?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There are different ways of entering it, from the left-hand side and from the right-hand side of the building. Also, it is possible to enter from the street of Izmedju Polaca, which is parallel to Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, so you won't have to tell us this kind of thing from left and from right. From the street called Izmedju Polaca, can your apartment be entered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's the only street that it can be entered from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which streets are perpendicular to Stradun, to the left and the right of the building where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Uska is the street on the right-hand side. And the other one -- I don't really pay attention to streets. I don't know. I know about different places but not the names of streets. Then also Miha Pracata is the street to the west, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically to tell me which streets are on the north of Stradun and on the west?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Uska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the east?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the south, which street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Izmedju Polaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The entrance into the building is from the southern side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Izmedju Polaca, the residential part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the first floor was where the then-Ms. Ruzica lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us how one reaches her apartment. Entering from Izmedju Polaca, how does one reach her apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: One opens the door and one goes upstairs. The stairs take a turn and then one comes to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many rooms are there in Ms. Ruzica's apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Three, including the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there are two rooms and the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. One is on the north side, the other one is on the south side, and between them is the bathroom where we hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How big is this apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: About 44 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is the first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the second floor is the apartment where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many rooms are there in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The same number of rooms, except that the ceiling is twice as high in comparison to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How big is your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Identical, since it is right above.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the actual layout of the rooms in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Similar to the layout on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is the bathroom in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Same place, like on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the third floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The third floor is somewhat different. There is a hall. To the north, there are two rooms and they are different in size, a bit different. And then from the hall, one goes to the attic. On the south side, facing Izmedju Polaca, is another room. And from that room, there is a hall, and that's where the entrance to the bathroom is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many windows of your wife's apartment face the street called Izmedju Polaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Two. Oh, you mean the street Izmedju Polaca? One from the hall and the other one from the east room. Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many windows are there facing Uska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: One window from the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What else is on the floor where your wife's apartment was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else on the first floor of the building at Izmedju Polaca number 10?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of answer you are expecting. Could you lead me to an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the first floor is your wife's apartment, 40 square metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else on the first floor of the building at Izmedju Polaca number 10?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There are two windows facing Stradun. They are identical, the two windows. And I've already referred to those facing south.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There are two windows facing Stradun, two facing Izmedju Polaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That's right, and one facing Uska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The situation is the same on the second floor, right, where your apartment is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, except that the windows are twice as big, since the ceiling is twice as high on that floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore the surface area of the building that we're talking about is 40 square metres, in view of the fact that there is nothing on the floors except apartments that are 40 square metres in size. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Each level has 40 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, your wife's room looking out on to the Izmedju Polaca street, how wide is that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That room is narrower by a staircase, compared to the one looking out on to the Stradun, half the size, in fact, half the surface area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many square metres would that be? How many metres wide would the room be looking out on to Izmedju Polaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Two metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How wide is the room facing out on to the Stradun? Would that make it four?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, four or five, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's the surface area of the part of the building inhabited by Mrs. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They are two identical halves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So apartments roughly 40 square metres there, too, one above the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means, Mr. A, that the block of buildings between Stradun, Uska Street, the street you don't know -- I'm telling you it's called Kaboge, Marojice Kaboge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the street Izmedju Polaca that you have marked on the map has a total surface area of 80 square metres. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. Of course I never measured it. But I would say that was roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know the surface area of the flat you live in. That's a basic fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the owner of the apartment, I'm just a tenant, so I never actually measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you live in that flat today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I'm on the third floor now. I live on the third floor today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you still don't know to the present day the surface area of the apartment you live in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, it's not important. I'm not going to sell the flat to make it important what the exact surface area is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you pay rent at all or anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Only electricity, water, et cetera, not rent at such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know the surface area, the size of the apartment you're paying the utilities for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not paying rent, so that wasn't an important point. I just pay the utilities, the amount of water and electricity and the rest that I use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who does the building belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It belongs to a professor. His name is Ivo Brangjolica and his sisters, Vjera and Mira, and two cousins, one of them lives in Belgrade and the other lives in Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you lived there free of charge, free of rent, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We have family ties, so I took care of the building for the owner, and this is the way he repays me for that, for taking care of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's just recapitulate, you didn't tell me how many windows look out on to Uska Street, on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: One, but it's double the size of the one on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the bathroom have any windows, the one you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, none of the bathrooms have windows. They are lodged between the walls of the two identical parts of the buildings, the one belonging to Mrs. Aleksic and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When the events of the 6th of December started, did you go to the bathroom straight away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I didn't myself. It was around about 6.00 o'clock. I would go in and leave it, but after 6.00 o'clock, as I have already said, until 7.00 o'clock, Ruzica and Mrs. Aleksic were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So where were you from 5.00 o'clock, when you woke up, where were you after that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I walked around going between those two rooms, the one facing Stradun, the one facing the Od Puca street, and the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you go into the bathroom yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: At about 7.00 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was Mrs. Aleksic and your wife, were they in the bathroom already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you yourself go in at 7.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I was obviously less afraid than they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And from that time on, once you had entered the bathroom, how long did you stay inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I remained there until about 9.00 o'clock. Or I would spend 20 minutes of every hour there, depending on the intensity of the projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that the projectiles fell every second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What made you decide to leave then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, judging by the explosion. If I thought they were falling further away into another part of town, then I would leave the bathroom. And as things got closer to my own building, I would go back into the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So was there any regularity in the explosions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know. You would have to ask the JNA that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you know when to leave the bathroom and when to go into it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: By the sounds I would decide what to do, whether they were closer or further, the projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Once you left the bathroom, for instance, what did you see upon leaving the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I'd take a peek out at the window -- I'd look through the window, actually. I didn't do that many times by noon -- actually, I would just look through the window and see the construction material falling off the roofs, the stones, the tiles, the wood, pieces of wood, the debris.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your window open, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. All the windows were open, because the explosions, any explosion, would shatter the window panes. And then that glass would be very dangerous to people falling down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your window was wide open, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. All the peripheral windows were wide open.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't have any shutters on the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The shutters were wide open, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was that what people did in the Old Town, all of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't know what others did. I'm telling you what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what about the people across the road in Uska Street or between -- or Izmedju Polaca Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Their windows were open, too, but I didn't notice people. They probably laid down -- were lying down in some spot or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So generally speaking, you would leave the bathroom when you felt that the intensity --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Around the building was smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around the building smaller, right. How many hits occurred around your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I didn't count them but a lot. In the whole of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your building and around it, how many hits? Let me put it this way. From the Izmedju Polaca Street, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Izmedju Polaca you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I don't remember. They did occur, but I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many? One? Two? 10? 20? 50? How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: My answer was that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many hits were there in Uska Street that your windows look out on to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were some hits. I can't tell you how many. I really don't know. I never counted them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I'm already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many hits were there from the northern side of your house facing Stradun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I remember that better, better how many hits there were in Stradun. In the whole of Stradun, there were roughly about 50 hits directly on to the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How were you able to remember that better? How do you know what happened on Stradun better, whereas you don't remember what happened in the streets going into -- leading up to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Because the Stradun is the walkway, the main street. And the narrow streets just serve you -- you just take them to get somewhere. But Stradun is the main strolling street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you have to go through Stradun into Uska Street to go into your own house, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you didn't see whether anything was damaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There was damage, yes, but I don't know how much, the extent of the damage. There was damage everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many shells fell in front of your house on the Stradun side? Not the whole of Stradun, just in front of your own house, the width of your own house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: On the pavement in front of the house, of my house, I would say about 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many fell on your house, hit your house, the left side of your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the shelling started at around 5.00 and that you took refuge in the bathroom and that you left the bathroom definitely at 8.00 o'clock in the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't use it after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Why were you in the bathroom until 8.00 o'clock at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Because that was the time until when you could hear the explosions. After 6.00 o'clock, the intensity subsided, and it completely stopped at 8.00 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So although the intensity became less after 6.00, you still spent two hours in the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. I would go in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when the shelling was strongest, according to your descriptions, you spent half the time in the bathroom and half the time outside of the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I spent 60 per cent of my time in the bathroom, I would say. That would be the rough ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody wounded in front of your house, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In front of my house, I didn't see anyone wounded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm loath to interrupt my friend. There is a matter which I wish to raise about evidence tomorrow. I apologise for not raising it with the legal officer before. Would it be an appropriate time, given that there's only a couple minutes to go, to do it now?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it convenient to break in your cross-examination now, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can this matter be raised with the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Preferably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Close the shutters. So we're going to have to come to an end of your evidence today and resume tomorrow. If you could leave with the orderly as soon as the shutters are down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for what I'm about to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's justification for that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to tomorrow's witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
